Dichotomy of Early and Late Phase Implicit Biases Can Provably Induce Grokking

Kaifeng Lyu Thanks: Equal Contribution Affiliation: Princeton University Email: klyu@cs.princeton.edu    Jikai Jin11 1 Code is available at https://github.com/vfleaking/grokking-dichotomy Affiliation: Stanford University Email: jkjin@stanford.edu    Zhiyuan Li Affiliation: Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago Email: zhiyuanli@ttic.edu    Simon S. Du Affiliation: University of Washington Email: ssdu@cs.washington.edu    Jason D. Lee Affiliation: Princeton University Email: jasonlee@princeton.edu    Wei Hu Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: vvh@umich.edu
Abstract

Recent work by Power et al. 2022 highlighted a surprising “grokking” phenomenon in learning arithmetic tasks: a neural net first “memorizes” the training set, resulting in perfect training accuracy but near-random test accuracy, and after training for sufficiently longer, it suddenly transitions to perfect test accuracy. This paper studies the grokking phenomenon in theoretical setups and shows that it can be induced by a dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases. Specifically, when training homogeneous neural nets with large initialization and small weight decay on both classification and regression tasks, we prove that the training process gets trapped at a solution corresponding to a kernel predictor for a long time, and then a very sharp transition to min-norm/max-margin predictors occurs, leading to a dramatic change in test accuracy.

1 Introduction

The generalization behavior of modern over-parameterized neural nets has been puzzling: these nets have the capacity to overfit the training set, and yet they frequently exhibit a small gap between training and test performance when trained by popular gradient-based optimizers. A common view now is that the network architectures and training pipelines can automatically induce regularization effects to avoid or mitigate overfitting throughout the training trajectory.

Recently, Power et al. 2022 discovered an even more perplexing generalization phenomenon called grokking: when training a neural net to learn modular arithmetic operations, it first “memorizes” the training set with zero training error and near-random test error, and then training for much longer leads to a sharp transition from no generalization to perfect generalization. See Section 2 for our reproduction of this phenomenon. Beyond modular arithmetic, grokking has been reported in learning group operations (Chughtai et al. 2023), learning sparse parity (Barak et al. 2022; Bhattamishra et al. 2023), learning greatest common divisor (Charton 2024), and image classification (Liu et al. 2023; Radhakrishnan et al. 2022).

Different viewpoints on the mechanism of grokking have been proposed, including the slingshot mechanism (cyclic phase transitions) (Thilak et al. 2022), random walk among minimizers (Millidge 2022), slow formulation of good representations (Liu et al. 2022), the scale of initialization (Liu et al. 2023), and the simplicity of the generalizable solution (Nanda et al. 2023; Varma et al. 2023). However, existing studies failed to address two crucial aspects for gaining a comprehensive understanding of grokking:

  1. 1.

    No prior work has rigorously proved grokking in a neural network setting.

  2. 2.

    No prior work has provided a quantitative explanation as to why the transition from memorization to generalization is often sharp, instead of gradual.

Our Contributions.

In this work, we address these limitations by identifying simple yet insightful theoretical setups where grokking with sharp transition can be rigorously proved and its mechanism can be intuitively understood. Our main intuition is that optimizers may implicitly induce different biases in early and late phases; grokking happens if the early phase bias implies an overfitting solution and late phase bias implies a generalizable solution.

More specifically, we focus on neural nets with large initialization and small weight decay. This is inspired by a recent work (Liu et al. 2023) showing that training with these two tricks can induce grokking on many tasks, even beyond learning modular arithmetic. Our theoretical analysis attributes this to the following dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases: the large initialization induces a very strong early phase implicit bias towards kernel predictors, but over time, it decays and competes with a late phase implicit bias towards min-norm/max-margin predictors induced by the small weight decay, resulting in a transition that turns out to be provably sharp in between.

This implicit bias result holds for homogeneous neural nets, a broad class of neural nets that include commonly used MLPs and CNNs with homogeneous activation. We further exemplify this dichotomy in sparse linear classification with diagonal linear nets and low-rank matrix completion with over-parameterized models, where we provide theory and experiments showing that the kernel predictor does not generalize well but the min-norm/max-margin predictors do, hence grokking happens (see Figures 1 and 3).

Based on these theoretical insights, we are able to construct examples where the early phase implicit bias leads to a generalizable solution, and the late phase bias leads to overfitting. This gives rise to a new phenomenon which we call “misgrokking”: a neural net first achieves perfect training and test accuracies, but training for a longer time leads to a sudden big drop in test accuracy. See Figure 1.

Our proof of the kernel regime in the early phase is related to the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime studied in the literature (Jacot et al. 2018; Chizat et al. 2019). However, our result is qualitatively different from existing NTK analyses in that in our setting, the weight norm changes significantly (due to weight decay), while in the usual NTK regime, the weight changes only by a small amount, and so does its norm. Our proof relies on a careful analysis of the norm and direction of the weight, which enables us to obtain a tight bound on the time spent in the kernel regime. This novel result of a kernel regime in homogeneous neural nets under weight decay may be of independent interest. We further analyze the late phase using a gradient convergence argument, and it turns out that a slightly longer time suffices for convergence to the max-margin/min-norm predictor, thus exhibiting a sharp transition between the two phases.

Concretely, our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    For training homogeneous neural nets with large initialization and small weight decay on classification and regression tasks, we prove a very sharp transition from optimal solutions of kernel SVM/regression to KKT solutions of global max-margin/min-norm problems associated with the neural net.

  2. 2.

    For classification and regression tasks respectively, we provide concrete examples with diagonal linear nets and overparameterized matrix completion, showing either grokking or misgrokking.

2 Motivating Experiment: Grokking in Modular Addition

In this section, we provide experiments to show that the initialization scale and weight decay are important factors in the grokking phenomenon, in the sense that enlarging the initialization scale or reducing the weight decay delays the sharp transition in test accuracy.

Grokking in Modular Addition.

Following many previous works (Nanda et al. 2023; Gromov 2023), we focus on modular addition, which belongs to the modular arithmetic tasks where the grokking phenomenon was first observed (Power et al. 2022). The task is to learn the addition operation over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}: randomly split {(a,b,c):a+b≡c(modp)}\{(a,b,c):a+b\equiv c\pmod{p}\} into training and test sets, and train a neural net on the training set to predict cc given input pair (a,b)(a,b). The grokking phenomenon has been observed in learning this task under many training regimes, including training transformers and MLPs on cross-entropy and squared loss with various optimizers (full-batch GD, SGD, Adam, AdamW, etc.) (Power et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2022; Thilak et al. 2022; Gromov 2023). For simplicity, we focus on a simple setting without involving too many confounding factors: training a two-layer ReLU net with full-batch GD. More specifically, we represent the input (a,b)∈ℤp×ℤp(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p} as the concatenation of the one-hot representations of aa and bb, resulting in an input vector 𝒙∈ℝ2​p{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2p}, and then the neural net processes the input as follows:

f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)=𝑾2​ReLU​(𝑾1​𝒙+𝒃1),f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}})={\bm{W}}_{2}\,\mathrm{ReLU}({\bm{W}}_{1}{\bm{x}}+{\bm{b}}_{1}), (1)

where 𝜽=(𝑾1,𝒃1,𝑾2){\bm{\theta}}=({\bm{W}}_{1},{\bm{b}}_{1},{\bm{W}}_{2}) is the parameter vector consisting of 𝑾1∈ℝh×2​p,𝒃1∈ℝh,𝑾2∈ℝp×h{\bm{W}}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times 2p},{\bm{b}}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{h},{\bm{W}}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times h}, hh is the width, and ReLU⁡(𝒗)\mathrm{ReLU}({\bm{v}}) stands for the ReLU activation that maps each entry viv_{i} of a vector 𝒗{\bm{v}} to max⁡{vi,0}\max\{v_{i},0\}. The neural net output f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)∈ℝpf({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}})\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is treated as logits and is fed into the standard cross-entropy loss in training. We set the modulus pp as 9797, the training data size as 40%40\% of the total number of data (p2p^{2}), the width hh as 10241024, the learning rate as 0.0020.002 and weight decay as 10−410^{-4}. Figure 2 successfully reproduces the grokking phenomenon: the training accuracy reaches 100%100\% in 10610^{6} steps while the test accuracy remains close to random guessing, but after training for one additional order of magnitude in the number of steps, the test accuracy suddenly jumps to 100%100\%.

A natural question is how this grokking phenomenon depends on the training tricks in the pipeline. Liu et al. 2023 showed that, empirically, using a large initialization scale and a small but non-zero weight decay can induce grokking on various tasks even beyond modular arithmetic, including image classification on MNIST and sentiment classification on IMDB. Indeed, our experiments on modular addition can confirm the importance of initialization scale and weight decay.

Effect of Initialization Scale.

To study the effect of initialization, we scale up the standard He initialization (He et al. 2015) by a factor of α>0\alpha>0, and then run the same training procedure. However, the model at large initialization produces a very large random number for each training sample, which induces training instability. To remove this confounding factor, we set the weights 𝑾2{\bm{W}}_{2} in the second layer to 𝟎{\bm{0}} so that the initial model output is always 00. Results in Figure 2 show that the sharp transition in test accuracy is delayed when α\alpha increases from 11 to 100100.

Effect of Weight Decay.

In Figure 2, we run experiments with different weight decay values. We observe that increasing weight decay makes the transition happen earlier. However, when weight decay surpasses a small threshold, the regularization strength can become so strong that it even hinders the optimization of the training loss and causes the training accuracy to collapse eventually. This collapse due to weight decay is also consistent with the observation in Lewkowycz and Gur-Ari 2020. Conversely, as weight decay decreases, the grokking phenomenon becomes more significant because now it takes more time for the test accuracy to exhibit the sharp transition. But the weight decay has to be non-zero: we will discuss in Section B.1 that training without weight decay leads to perfect generalization in the end, but the transition in test accuracy is no longer sharp.

Explanation?

Liu et al. 2023 built their intuition upon an empirical observation from Fort and Scherlis 2019: there is a narrow range of weight norm, called Goldilocks zone, where the generalization inside the zone is better than the outside. It is argued that the weight norm can take a longer time to enter this Goldilocks zone when training with a larger initial weight norm or smaller weight decay, hence causing the delayed generalization. However, Fort and Scherlis 2019; Liu et al. 2023 did not provide much explanation on why such a narrow Goldilocks zone could exist in the first place. When talking about MLPs and CNNs with ReLU activation, which are commonly used in practice, this becomes even more mysterious: the output functions f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) of these neural nets are homogeneous to their parameters, i.e., f⁡(c​𝜽,𝒙)=cL​f​(𝜽,𝒙)f(c{\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}})=c^{L}f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) for all c>0c>0 (Lyu and Li 2020; Ji and Telgarsky 2020a; Kunin et al. 2023). As a result, it is impossible to explain the effect of norm just from the expressive power, since all classifiers that can be represented with a certain norm can also be represented by all other norms. This motivates us to dive deep into the training dynamics in grokking via rigorous theoretical analysis.

3 Grokking with Large Initialization and Small Weight Decay

In this section, we present our theory on homogeneous neural nets with large initialization and small weight decay, which attributes grokking to a dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases.

3.1 Theoretical Setup

We focus on training models for classification and regression. Let 𝒟X\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{X}} be the input distribution. For every input 𝒙∼𝒟X{\bm{x}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{X}}, let y∗​(𝒙)y^{*}({\bm{x}}) be the classification/regression target of 𝒙{\bm{x}}. We parameterize the model with 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} and use f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) to denote the model output on input 𝒙{\bm{x}}. We train the model by optimizing an empirical loss on a dataset {(𝒙i,yi)}i=1n\{({\bm{x}}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} where the data points are drawn i.i.d. as 𝒙i∼𝒟X,yi=y∗​(𝒙i){\bm{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{X}},y_{i}=y^{*}({\bm{x}}_{i}). For each i∈[n]i\in[n], we write fi​(𝜽):=f⁡(𝜽,𝒙i)f_{i}({\bm{\theta}}):=f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}_{i}) for short. We assume the model is homogeneous with respect to its parameters 𝜽{\bm{\theta}}, a common assumption in analyzing neural networks (Lyu and Li 2020; Ji and Telgarsky 2020a; Telgarsky 2023; Woodworth et al. 2020).

Assumption 3.1.

For all 𝐱{\bm{x}}, f⁡(𝛉,𝐱)f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) is LL-homogeneous (i.e., fi​(c​𝛉)=cL​fi​(𝛉)f_{i}(c{\bm{\theta}})=c^{L}f_{i}({\bm{\theta}}) for all c>0c>0) and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2}-smooth with respect to 𝛉{\bm{\theta}}.

The two-layer net in our motivating experiment and other MLPs and CNNs with ReLU activation are indeed LL-homogeneous. However, we also need to assume the 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2}-smoothness to ease the definition and analysis of gradient flow, which excludes the use of any non-smooth activation. This can be potentially addressed by defining and analyzing gradient flow via Clarke’s subdifferential (Clarke 1975; Clarke 2001; Lyu and Li 2020; Ji and Telgarsky 2020a), but we choose to make this assumption for simplicity. Note that our concrete examples of grokking on sparse linear classification and matrix completion indeed satisfy this assumption.

As motivated in Section 2, we consider training with large initialization and small weight decay. Mathematically, we start training from α​𝜽¯init\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}, where 𝜽¯init∈ℝd\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a fixed vector and α\alpha is a large factor controlling the initialization scale. We also assume a small but non-zero weight decay λ>0\lambda>0. To study the asymptotics more conveniently, we regard λ\lambda as a function of α\alpha with order λ⁡(α)=Θ⁡(α−p)\lambda(\alpha)=\Theta(\alpha^{-p}) for some positive p=Θ⁡(1)p=\Theta(1).

To avoid loss explosion at initialization, we deterministically set or randomly sample 𝜽¯init\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}} in a way that the initial output of the model is zero. This can be done by setting the last layer weights to zero (same as our experiments in Section 2), using the symmetrized initialization in Chizat et al. 2019, or using the “difference trick” in Hu et al. 2020. This zero-output initialization is also used in many previous studies of implicit bias (Chizat et al. 2019; Woodworth et al. 2020; Moroshko et al. 2020) for the sake of mathematical simplicity. We note that our analysis should be easily extended to random initialization with small outputs, just as in Chizat et al. 2019; Arora et al. 2019b.

Assumption 3.2.

f⁡(𝜽¯init,𝒙)=0f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})=0 for all 𝐱{\bm{x}}.

We define the vanilla training loss as the average over the loss values of each individual sample:

ℒ⁡(𝜽)=1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(fi​(𝜽),yi).\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(f_{i}({\bm{\theta}});y_{i}). (2)

With weight decay λ\lambda, it becomes the following regularized training loss:

ℒλ​(𝜽)=ℒ⁡(𝜽)+λ2​‖𝜽‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}})=\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}})+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|{\bm{\theta}}\|_{2}^{2}. (3)

For simplicity, in this paper, we consider minimizing the loss via gradient flow d​𝜽d​t=−∇ℒλ​(𝜽)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\bm{\theta}}}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}), which is the continuous counterpart of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent when the learning rate goes to 00. We use 𝜽⁡(t,𝜽0){\bm{\theta}}(t;{\bm{\theta}}_{0}) to denote the parameter at time tt by running gradient flow from 𝜽0{\bm{\theta}}_{0}, and we write 𝜽⁡(t){\bm{\theta}}(t) when the initialization 𝜽0{\bm{\theta}}_{0} is clear from the context.

3.2 Grokking in Classification

In this subsection, we study the grokking phenomenon on classification tasks. For simplicity, we restrict to binary classification problems, where y∗​(𝒙)∈{−1,+1}y^{*}({\bm{x}})\in\{-1,+1\}. While in practice it is standard to use the logistic loss ℓ⁡(y^,y)=log⁡(1+e−y​y^)\ell(\hat{y},y)=\log(1+e^{-y\hat{y}}) (a.k.a. binary cross-entropy loss), we follow the implicit bias literature to analyze the exponential loss ℓ⁡(y^,y)=e−y​y^\ell(\hat{y};y)=e^{-y\hat{y}} as a simple surrogate, which has the same tail behavior as the logistic loss when y​y^→+∞y\hat{y}\to+\infty and thus usually leads to the same implicit bias (Soudry et al. 2018; Nacson et al. 2019b; Lyu and Li 2020; Chizat and Bach 2020).

By carefully analyzing the training dynamics, we rigorously prove that there is a sharp transition around 1λ​log⁡α\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha. Before this point, gradient flow fits the training data perfectly while maintaining the parameter direction within a local region near the initial direction, which causes the classifier to behave like a kernel classifier based on Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) (Jacot et al. 2018; Arora et al. 2019b; Arora et al. 2019c). After the transition, however, the gradient flow escapes the local region and makes efforts to maximize the margin. Following the nomenclature in (Moroshko et al. 2020), we call the first regime the kernel regime and the second regime the rich regime. The key difference to the existing works analyzing the kernel and rich regimes (Moroshko et al. 2020; Telgarsky 2023) is that the transition in our case is provably sharp, which is a crucial ingredient for the grokking phenomenon.

3.2.1 Kernel Regime

First, we show that gradient flow gets stuck in the kernel regime over the initial period of 1−cλ​log⁡α\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, where the model behaves as if it were optimizing over a linearized model. More specifically, for all 𝒙{\bm{x}}, we define ∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙)\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}}) as the NTK feature of 𝒙{\bm{x}}. As we are considering over-parameterized models, where the dimension of 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} is larger than the number of data nn, it is natural to assume that the NTK features of the training data are linearly separable (Ji and Telgarsky 2020b; Telgarsky 2023):

Assumption 3.3.

There exists 𝐡{\bm{h}} such that yi​⟨∇fi​(𝛉¯init),𝐡⟩>0y_{i}\left\langle{\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})},{{\bm{h}}}\right\rangle>0 for all i∈[n]i\in[n].

Let 𝒉ntk∗{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}} be the unit vector so that a linear classifier with weight 𝒉ntk∗{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}} can attain the max L2L^{2}-margin on the NTK features of the training data, {(∇fi​(𝜽¯init),yi)}i=1n\{(\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}),y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}, and γntk\gamma_{\mathrm{ntk}} be the corresponding L2L^{2}-margin. That is, 𝒉ntk∗{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}} is the unique unit vector that points to the direction of the unique optimal solution to the following constrained optimization problem:

For any all constants c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), letting Tc−​(α):=1−cλ​log⁡αT^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha):=\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, it holds that

The large scaling factor αL​e−L​λ​t\alpha^{L}e^{-L\lambda t} above enables fitting the dataset even when the change in direction eλ​tα​𝜽−𝜽¯init\tfrac{e^{\lambda t}}{\alpha}{\bm{\theta}}-\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}} is very small. 3.2.2 Rich Regime

Next, we show that continuing the gradient flow for a slightly long time to time 1+cλ​log⁡α\frac{1+c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, it is able to escape the kernel regime. More specifically, consider the following constrained optimization problem that aims at maximizing the margin of the predictor f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) on the training data {(𝒙i,yi)}i=1n\{({\bm{x}}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}:

min12​‖𝜽‖22s.t.yi​fi​(𝜽)≥1,∀i∈[n].\displaystyle\min\quad\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{\theta}}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_{i}f_{i}({\bm{\theta}})\geq 1,\quad\forall i\in[n]. (R1)

Then we have the following directional convergence result:

Theorem 3.5.

For all constants c>0c>0 and for every sequence {αk}k≥1\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} with αk→+∞\alpha_{k}\to+\infty, letting Tc+​(α):=1+cλ​log⁡αT^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha):=\frac{1+c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, there exists a time sequence {tk}k≥1\{t_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} such that 1λ​log⁡αk≤tk≤Tc+​(αk)\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha_{k}\leq t_{k}\leq T^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha_{k}) and every limit point of {𝛉⁡(tk,αk​𝛉¯init)‖𝛉⁡(tk,αk​𝛉¯init)‖2:k≥1}\left\{\frac{{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};\alpha_{k}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})}{\|{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};\alpha_{k}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}}:k\geq 1\right\} is along the direction of a KKT point of (R1).

For the problem Equation R1, the KKT condition is a first-order necessary condition for global optimality, but it is not sufficient in general since fi​(𝜽)f_{i}({\bm{\theta}}) can be highly non-convex. Nonetheless, since gradient flow can easily get trapped at spurious minima with only first-order information, the KKT condition is widely adopted as a surrogate for global optimality in theoretical analysis (Lyu and Li 2020; Wang et al. 2021; Kunin et al. 2023).

Key Proof Insight.

The key is to use the loss convergence and norm decay bounds from the kernel regime as a starting point to obtain a small upper bound for the gradient ∇ℒλ​(𝜽)\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}). Then we connect the gradient upper bounds with KKT conditions. See Section C.3 for the proof.

3.2.3 Example: Linear Classification with Diagonal Linear Nets

Now, we exemplify how our implicit bias results imply a sharp transition in test accuracy in a concrete setting: training diagonal linear nets for linear classification. Let 𝒟X\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{X}} be a distribution over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and y∗​(𝒙)=sign⁡(⟨𝒘∗,𝒙⟩)∈{±1}y^{*}({\bm{x}})=\sign(\left\langle{{\bm{w}}^{*}},{{\bm{x}}}\right\rangle)\in\{\pm 1\} be the ground-truth target for binary classification, where 𝒘∗∈ℝd{\bm{w}}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is an unknown vector. Following Moroshko et al. 2020, we consider training a so-called two-layer “diagonal” linear net to learn y∗y^{*}. On input 𝒙∈ℝd{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the model outputs the following function f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}), where 𝜽:=(𝒖,𝒗)∈ℝd×ℝd≃ℝ2​d{\bm{\theta}}:=({\bm{u}},{\bm{v}})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{2d} is the model parameter.

f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)=∑k=1duk2​xk−∑k=1dvk2​xk.\displaystyle f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}})=\sum_{k=1}^{d}u_{k}^{2}x_{k}-\sum_{k=1}^{d}v_{k}^{2}x_{k}. (4)

This model is considered a diagonal net because it can be seen as a sparsely-connected two-layer net with 2​d2d hidden neurons, each of which only inputs and outputs a single scalar. More specifically, the input 𝒙{\bm{x}} is first expanded to an 2​d2d-dimensional vector (𝒙,−𝒙)({\bm{x}},-{\bm{x}}). Then the kk-th hidden neuron in the first half inputs xkx_{k} and outputs uk​xku_{k}x_{k}, and the kk-th hidden neuron in the second half inputs −xk-x_{k} and outputs vk​xkv_{k}x_{k}. The output neuron in the second layer shares the same weights as the hidden neurons and takes a weighted sum over the hidden neuron outputs according to their weights: f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)=∑k=1duk⋅(uk⋅xk)+∑k=1dvk⋅(vk⋅(−xk))f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}})=\sum_{k=1}^{d}u_{k}\cdot(u_{k}\cdot x_{k})+\sum_{k=1}^{d}v_{k}\cdot(v_{k}\cdot(-x_{k})). Note that the model output is always linear with the input. For convenience, we can write f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)=⟨𝒘⁡(𝜽),𝒙⟩f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}})=\left\langle{{\bm{w}}({\bm{\theta}})},{{\bm{x}}}\right\rangle with effective weight 𝒘⁡(𝜽):=𝒖⊙2−𝒗⊙2{\bm{w}}({\bm{\theta}}):={\bm{u}}^{\odot 2}-{\bm{v}}^{\odot 2}.

In this setup, we can understand the early and late phase implicit biases very concretely. We start training from a large initialization: 𝜽⁡(0)=α​𝜽¯init{\bm{\theta}}(0)=\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}, where α>0\alpha>0 controls the initialization scale and 𝜽¯init=(𝟏,𝟏)\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}=({\bm{1}},{\bm{1}}). That is, uk=vk=αu_{k}=v_{k}=\alpha for all 1≤k≤d1\leq k\leq d at t=0t=0. As noted in Moroshko et al. 2020, the kernel feature for each data point is ∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙)=(2​𝒙,−2​𝒙)\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})=(2{\bm{x}},-2{\bm{x}}), so the max L2L^{2}-margin kernel classifier is the max L2L^{2}-margin linear classifier. This leads to the following corollary:

Corollary 3.6 (Diagonal linear nets, kernel regime).

Let Tc−​(α):=1−cλ​log⁡αT^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha):=\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha. For all constants c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), as α→+∞\alpha\to+\infty, the normalized effective weight vector 𝐰⁡(𝛉⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝛉¯init))‖𝐰⁡(𝛉⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝛉¯init))‖2\frac{{\bm{w}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))}{\|{\bm{w}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))\|_{2}} converges to the max L2L^{2}-margin direction, namely 𝐰2∗:=arg​max𝐰∈𝒮d−1⁡{mini∈[n]⁡yi​⟨𝐰,𝐱i⟩}{\bm{w}}^{*}_{2}:=\argmax_{{\bm{w}}\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}\{\min_{i\in[n]}y_{i}\langle{{\bm{w}}},{{\bm{x}}_{i}}\rangle\}.

In contrast, if we train slightly longer from Tc−​(α)T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha) to Tc+​(α)T^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha), we can obtain a KKT point of (R1).

Corollary 3.7 (Diagonal linear nets, rich regime).

Let Tc+​(α):=1+cλ​log⁡αT^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha):=\frac{1+c}{\lambda}\log\alpha. For all constants c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), and for every sequence {αk}k≥1\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} with αk→+∞\alpha_{k}\to+\infty, there exists a time sequence {tk}k≥1\{t_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} such that 1λ​log⁡αk≤tk≤Tc+​(αk)\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha_{k}\leq t_{k}\leq T^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha_{k}) and every limit point of {𝛉⁡(tk,αk​𝛉¯init)‖𝛉⁡(tk,αk​𝛉¯init)‖2:k≥1}\left\{\frac{{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};\alpha_{k}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})}{\|{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};\alpha_{k}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}}:k\geq 1\right\} is along the direction of a KKT point of the problem min⁡‖𝐮‖22+‖𝐯‖22\min\|{\bm{u}}\|_{2}^{2}+\|{\bm{v}}\|_{2}^{2} s.t. yi​⟨𝐮⊙2−𝐯⊙2,𝐱i⟩≥1y_{i}\langle{{\bm{u}}^{\odot 2}-{\bm{v}}^{\odot 2}},{{\bm{x}}_{i}}\rangle\geq 1.

As noted in these two works, in the diagonal linear case, optimizing (R1) to the global optimum is equivalent to finding the max L1L^{1}-margin linear classifier: min⁡‖𝒘‖1\min\|{\bm{w}}\|_{1} s.t. yi​⟨𝒘,𝒙i⟩≥1,∀i∈[n]y_{i}\langle{{\bm{w}}},{{\bm{x}}_{i}}\rangle\geq 1,\forall i\in[n], or equivalently, 𝒘1∗:=arg​max𝐰∈𝒮d−1⁡{mini∈[n]⁡yi​⟨𝐰,𝐱i⟩}{\bm{w}}^{*}_{1}:=\argmax_{{\bm{w}}\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}\{\min_{i\in[n]}y_{i}\langle{{\bm{w}}},{{\bm{x}}_{i}}\rangle\}. Therefore, our theory suggests a sharp transition at time 1λ​log⁡α\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha from max L2L^{2}-margin linear classifier to max L1L^{1}-margin linear classifier.

While this corollary only shows KKT conditions rather than global optimality, we believe that one may be able to obtain the global optimality using insights from existing analysis of training diagonal linear nets without weight decay (Gunasekar et al. 2018b; Moroshko et al. 2020).

Empirical Validation: Grokking.

As it is well known that maximizing the L1L^{1}-margin can better encourage sparsity than maximizing the L2L^{2}-margin, our theory predicts that the grokking phenomenon can be observed in training diagonal linear nets for kk-sparse linear classification. To verify this, we specifically consider the following task: sample nn data points uniformly from {±1}d\{\pm 1\}^{d} for a very large dd, and let the ground truth be a linear classifier with a kk-sparse weight, where the non-zero coordinates are sampled uniformly from {±1}k\{\pm 1\}^{k}. Applying standard generalization bounds based on Rademacher complexity can show that the max L2L^{2}-margin linear classifier needs 𝒪⁡(k​d)\mathcal{O}(kd) to generalize, while the max L1L^{1}-margin linear classifier only needs 𝒪⁡(k2​log⁡d)\mathcal{O}(k^{2}\log d). See Section E.2 for the proof. This suggests that the grokking phenomenon can be observed in this setting. In Figure 1, we run experiments with n=256,d=105,k=3n=256,d=10^{5},k=3, large initialization with initial parameter norm 128128, and small weight decay λ=0.001\lambda=0.001. As expected, we observe the grokking phenomenon: in the early phase, the net fits the training set very quickly but fails to generalize; after a sharp transition in the late phase, the test accuracy becomes 100%100\%.

Empirical Validation: Misgrokking.

From the above example, we can see that grokking can be induced by the mismatch between the early-phase implicit bias and data and a good match between the late-phase implicit bias and data. However, this match and mismatch can largely depend on data. Conversely, if we consider the case where the labels in the linear classification problem are generated by a linear classifier with a large L2L^{2}-margin, the early phase implicit bias can make the neural net generalize easily, but the late phase implicit bias can destroy this good generalization since the ground-truth weight vector may not have a large L1L^{1}-margin. To justify this, we first sample a unit-norm vector 𝒘∗{\bm{w}}^{*}, then sample a dataset from the distribution (𝒙,y)∼(𝒛+γ2​sign⁡(⟨𝒛,𝒘∗⟩)​𝒘∗,sign⁡(⟨𝒛,𝒘∗⟩)CLOSE({\bm{x}},y)\sim({\bm{z}}+\frac{\gamma}{2}\sign(\langle{{\bm{z}}},{{\bm{w}}^{*}}\rangle){\bm{w}}^{*},\sign(\langle{{\bm{z}}},{{\bm{w}}^{*}}\rangle), where 𝒛∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d){\bm{z}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\bm{0}},{\bm{I}}_{d}) (i.e., a Gaussian distribution that is separated by a margin in the middle). We take γ=25\gamma=25 and sample n=32n=32 points. Indeed, we observe a phenomenon which we call “misgrokking”: the neural net first fits the training set and achieves 100%100\% test accuracy, and then after training for sufficiently longer, the test accuracy drops to nearly 50%50\%. See Figure 1.

3.3 Grokking in Regression

In this subsection, we study the grokking phenomenon on regression tasks with squared loss ℓ⁡(y^,y)=(y^−y)2\ell(\hat{y},y)=(\hat{y}-y)^{2}. Paralleling the classification setting, we analyze the behavior of gradient flow in both kernel and rich regimes, and show that there is a sharp transition around 1λ​log⁡α\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha.

3.3.1 Kernel Regime

Similar to the classification setting, we first show that gradient flow gets stuck in the kernel regime over the initial period of 1−cλ​log⁡α\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha time. For all 𝒙{\bm{x}}, we define ∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙)\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}}) as the NTK feature of 𝒙{\bm{x}}. For over-parameterized models, where the dimension of 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} is larger than the number of data nn, we make the following natural assumption that is also widely used in the literature (Du et al. 2019b; Chizat et al. 2019; Arora et al. 2019b):

Assumption 3.8.

The NTK features of training samples {∇f​(𝛉¯init,𝐱)}i=1n\{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})\}_{i=1}^{n} are linearly independent.

Now we let 𝒉ntk∗{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}} be the vector with minimum norm such that the linear predictor 𝒈↦⟨𝒈,𝒉⟩{\bm{g}}\mapsto\left\langle{{\bm{g}}},{{\bm{h}}}\right\rangle perfectly fits {(∇fi​(𝜽¯init),yi)}i=1n\{(\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}),y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}. That is, 𝒉ntk∗{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}} is the solution to the following constrained optimization problem:

min12​‖𝒉‖22s.t.⟨∇fi​(𝜽¯init),𝒉⟩=yi,∀i∈[n].\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \min\quad\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{h}}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\langle{\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})},{{\bm{h}}}\right\rangle=y_{i},\quad\forall i\in[n].\end{aligned} (K2)

Then we have the following result that is analogous to Theorem 3.4. See Section C.2 for the proof.

Theorem 3.9.

For all constants c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), letting Tc−​(α):=1−cλ​log⁡αT^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha):=\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, it holds that

∀𝒙∈ℝd:limα→+∞f⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init),𝒙)=⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝒉ntk∗⟩.\displaystyle\forall{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\qquad\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}f({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}});{\bm{x}})=\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}}}\right\rangle.

3.3.2 Rich Regime

Similar to the classification setting, we then show that gradient flow is able to escape the kernel regime at time 1+cλ​log⁡α\frac{1+c}{\lambda}\log\alpha. Specifically, consider the following constrained optimization problem that searches for the parameter with the minimum norm that can perfectly fit the training data:

min12​‖𝜽‖22s.t.fi​(𝜽)=yi,∀i∈[n].\displaystyle\min\quad\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{\theta}}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad f_{i}({\bm{\theta}})=y_{i},\quad\forall i\in[n]. (R2)

Then we have the following convergence result. See Section D.2 for the proof.

Theorem 3.10.

For any constant c>0c>0, letting Tc+​(α):=1+cλ​log⁡αT^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha):=\frac{1+c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, for any sequence of {αk}k≥1\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} with αk→+∞\alpha_{k}\to+\infty, there exists a time sequence {tk}k≥1\{t_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} satisfying 1λ​log⁡αk≤tk≤Tc+​(αk)\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha_{k}\leq t_{k}\leq T^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha_{k}), such that ‖𝛉⁡(tk,αk​𝛉¯init)‖2\|{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};\alpha_{k}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2} are uniformly bounded and that every limit point of {𝛉⁡(tk,αk​𝛉¯init):k≥1}\left\{{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};\alpha_{k}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}):k\geq 1\right\} is a KKT point of (R2).

3.3.3 Example: Overparameterized Matrix Completion

As an example, we consider the matrix completion problem of recovering a low-rank symmetric matrix based on partial observations of its entries. Specifically, we let 𝑿∗∈ℝd×d{\bm{X}}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be the ground-truth symmetric matrix with rank r≪dr\ll d and we observe a (random) set of entries indexed by Ω⊆[d]×[d]\Omega\subseteq[d]\times[d]. In this setting, the input distribution 𝒟X\mathcal{D}_{X} is the uniform distribution on the finite set [d]×[d][d]\times[d]. For every input 𝒙=(i,j)∼𝒟X{\bm{x}}=(i,j)\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}, y∗​(𝒙)=⟨𝑷𝒙,𝑿∗⟩y^{*}({\bm{x}})=\left\langle{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{x}}},{\bm{X}}^{*}\right\rangle where 𝑷x=𝒆i​𝒆j⊤{\bm{P}}_{x}={\bm{e}}_{i}{\bm{e}}_{j}^{\top}.

Following previous works (Arora et al. 2019a; Razin and Cohen 2020; Woodworth et al. 2020; Li et al. 2021), we solve the matrix completion problem using the matrix factorization approach, i.e., we parameterize a matrix as 𝑾=𝑼​𝑼⊤−𝑽​𝑽⊤{\bm{W}}={\bm{U}}{\bm{U}}^{\top}-{\bm{V}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}, where 𝑼,𝑽∈ℝd×d{\bm{U}},{\bm{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, and optimize 𝑼,𝑽{\bm{U}},{\bm{V}} so that 𝑾{\bm{W}} matches with the ground truth on observed entries. This can be viewed a neural net that is parameterized by 𝜽=(vec⁡(𝑼),vec⁡(𝑽))∈ℝ2​d2{\bm{\theta}}=(\mathrm{vec}({\bm{U}}),\mathrm{vec}({\bm{V}}))\in\mathbb{R}^{2d^{2}} and outputs f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)=⟨𝑷𝒙,𝑾⁡(𝜽)⟩f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}})=\left\langle{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{x}}},{\bm{W}}({\bm{\theta}})\right\rangle given 𝒙=(i,j){\bm{x}}=(i,j), where 𝑾⁡(𝜽):=𝑼​𝑼⊤−𝑽​𝑽⊤{\bm{W}}({\bm{\theta}}):={\bm{U}}{\bm{U}}^{\top}-{\bm{V}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}. It is easy to see that f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) is 22-homogeneous, satisfying 3.1. Given a dataset {(𝒙i,yi)}i=1n\{({\bm{x}}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}, we consider using gradient flow to minimize the ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized square loss defined in Equation 3 which can be equivalently written as

ℒ⁡(𝜽)=1n​∑i=1n(f⁡(𝜽,𝒙i)−yi)2+λ2​(‖𝑼‖F2+‖𝑽‖F2).\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}_{i})-y_{i}\right)^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\left(\|{\bm{U}}\|_{F}^{2}+\|{\bm{V}}\|_{F}^{2}\right). (5)

In the kernel regime, Theorem 3.9 implies the following result for identity initialization.

Corollary 3.11 (Matrix completion, kernel regime).

Let 𝛉¯init:=(vec⁡(𝐈),vec⁡(𝐈))\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}:=(\mathrm{vec}({\bm{I}}),\mathrm{vec}({\bm{I}})). For all constants c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), letting Tc−​(α)=1−cλ​log⁡αT_{c}^{-}(\alpha)=\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, it holds for all (i,j)∈[d]×[d](i,j)\in[d]\times[d] that

limα→+∞[𝑾(𝜽(Tc−(α);α𝜽¯init))]i​j={𝑿i​j∗if ​(i,j)∈Ω​ or ​(j,i)∈Ω,0otherwise.\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\left[{\bm{W}}({\bm{\theta}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))\right]_{ij}=\left\{\begin{aligned} {\bm{X}}_{ij}^{*}\quad&\text{if }(i,j)\in\Omega\text{ or }(j,i)\in\Omega,\\ 0\quad&\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.

In other words, in the kernel regime, while GD is able to fit the observed entries, it always fills the unobserved entries with 00, leading to a significant failure in recovering the matrix.

In the rich regime, Theorem 3.10 implies that the solution transitions sharply near 1λ​log⁡α\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha to a KKT point of the norm minimization problem. If this KKT point is globally optimal, then it is known that 𝑾⁡(𝜽){\bm{W}}({\bm{\theta}}) is the minimum nuclear norm solution to the matrix completion problem: min⁡‖𝑾‖∗\min\|{\bm{W}}\|_{*} s.t. 𝑾=𝑾⊤{\bm{W}}={\bm{W}}^{\top}, 𝑾i​j=𝑿i​j∗,∀(i,j)∈Ω{\bm{W}}_{ij}={\bm{X}}^{*}_{ij},\forall(i,j)\in\Omega (Ding et al. 2022, Theorem 3.2). It is known that the minimum nuclear norm solution can recover the ground truth with very small errors when 𝒪~​(d​log2​d)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\log^{2}d) entries are observed (Theorem F.5).

Although it is not proved that this KKT point is globally optimal, the following theorem provides positive evidence by showing that gradient flow eventually converges global minima and recovers the ground truth, if the time is not limited around 1λ​log⁡α\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha.

Theorem 3.12 (Matrix completion, rich regime).

Suppose that rank⁡(𝐗∗)=r=𝒪⁡(1)\mathrm{rank}{({\bm{X}}^{*})}=r=\mathcal{O}(1) and 𝐗∗=𝐕𝐗∗​𝚺𝐗∗​𝐕𝐗∗⊤{\bm{X}}^{*}={\bm{V}}_{{\bm{X}}^{*}}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{{\bm{X}}^{*}}{\bm{V}}_{{\bm{X}}^{*}}^{\top} is a SVD of 𝐗∗{\bm{X}}^{*}, where each row of 𝐕𝐗∗{\bm{V}}_{{\bm{X}}^{*}} has ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm bounded by μd\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{d}}. If the number of observed entries satisfies N≳μ4​d​log2​dN\gtrsim\mu^{4}d\log^{2}d, then for any σ>0\sigma>0, the gradient flow trajectory (𝛉⁡(t))t≥0({\bm{\theta}}(t))_{t\geq 0} for Equation 5 starting from random initialization (𝐔(0))i​j,(𝐕(0))i​j∼i.i.d𝒩(α𝟙{i=j},σ2)({\bm{U}}(0))_{ij},({\bm{V}}(0))_{ij}\overset{i.i.d}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\alpha\mathbbm{1}\{i=j\},\sigma^{2}) converges to a global minimizer 𝛉∞{\bm{\theta}}_{\infty} of ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}. Moreover, ‖𝐖⁡(𝛉∞)−𝐗∗‖F≲λ​‖𝐗∗‖∗​μ2​log⁡d\|{\bm{W}}({\bm{\theta}}_{\infty})-{\bm{X}}^{*}\|_{F}\lesssim\sqrt{\lambda\|{\bm{X}}^{*}\|_{*}}\mu^{2}\log d with probability ≥1−d−3\geq 1-d^{-3}.

Remark 3.13.

The small random perturbation to the identity initialization (α​𝐈,α​𝐈)(\alpha{\bm{I}},\alpha{\bm{I}}) in the above theorem is needed to guarantee that gradient flow does not get stuck at saddle points and thus converges to global minimizers almost surely. By the continuity of the gradient flow trajectory w.r.t. initialization, the conclusion of Corollary 3.11 still holds if σ=σ⁡(α)\sigma=\sigma(\alpha) is sufficiently small.

Empirical Validation.

We verify our theory on a simple algorithmic task: matrix completion for the multiplication table. Here, the multiplication table refers to a matrix 𝑿∗{\bm{X}}^{*} where the (i,j)(i,j)-entry is i​j/d2ij/d^{2}. It is easy to see that this matrix is of rank-11 since 𝑿∗=𝒖​𝒖⊤{\bm{X}}^{*}={\bm{u}}{\bm{u}}^{\top} for 𝒖=(0,1d,2d,…,d−1d){\bm{u}}=(0,\frac{1}{d},\frac{2}{d},\dots,\frac{d-1}{d}). This means the late phase bias can complete the matrix with few observed entries; however, the early phase bias fills every unobserved entry with 00, leading to a large test loss. This dichotomy of implicit biases implies grokking. To check this, we set d=97d=97 and randomly choose 5%5\% of the entries as the training set. We run GD with initialization scale α=10\alpha=10, learning rate η=0.1\eta=0.1, weight decay 10−410^{-4}. Figure 3 shows that grokking indeed happens: GD takes ∼101\sim 10^{1} steps to minimize the training loss, but the sharp transition in test loss occurs only after ∼106\sim 10^{6} steps.

4 Conclusion

In this paper, we show that the grokking phenomenon provably occurs in several setups. Our results suggest that the sharp transition in test accuracy may stem from a dichotomy of implicit biases between the early and late training phases. While the early phase bias guides the optimizer to overfitting solutions, it is quickly corrected when the late phase bias takes effect.

Some limitations of our work are as follows. First, our work only studies the training dynamics with large initialization and small weight decay, but these may not be the only source of the dichotomy of the implicit biases. We further discuss in Appendix B that the late phase implicit bias can also be induced by implicit margin maximization and sharpness reduction, though the transition may not be as sharp as the weight decay case. Also, our work focuses on understanding the cause of grokking but does not study how to make neural nets generalize without so much delay in time. We leave it to future work to explore the other sources of grokking and practical methods to eliminate grokking.

Appendix A Additional Related Works

Identifying Mechanisms that Cause Grokking.

Some works attempted to identify mechanisms that cause grokking through experiments. Davies et al. 2022 hypothesized that both grokking and double descent are the result of the existence of two patterns: one pattern is faster to learn but generalizes poorly, and the other pattern is slower to learn but generalizes well. However, it is unclear how these notions can be rigorously defined for general training dynamics. Similar to the work of Liu et al. 2023 that we discussed in Section 2, Varma et al. 2023 hypothesized that grokking happens when the generalizable solutions have a smaller parameter norm than the overfitting solutions, but the former takes a longer time to learn. They also demonstrated that violating a part of this condition indeed changes the generalization behavior from grokking to “ungrokking” and “semi-grokking”, two interesting phenomena they named in the paper. For training with adaptive gradient methods, Thilak et al. 2022 identified the Slingshot mechanism, which refers to a cyclic behavior of the last-layer parameter norm that empirically causes grokking. Notsawo Jr et al. 2023 also discussed a similar relationship between the oscillations in training loss and grokking. For the task of learning sparse parity, Merrill et al. 2023 empirically observed that the number of active neurons significantly decrease as the test accuracy starts to improve. While many explanations of grokking may make sense intuitively, none of these works provides rigorous justification their claims with mathematical analysis for neural net training, while our work is grounded by theoretical analyses of implicit biases in the kernel and rich regimes.

Progress Measures of Grokking.

Efforts have been made to find progress measures that are improving smoothly and are predictive of the time to perfect generalization. Nanda et al. 2023, Chughtai et al. 2023, Gromov 2023 focused on the tasks of learning modular arithmetic or more general group operations, and attempted to reverse engineer the weights of neural nets after grokking. It was found that the weights can exhibit special structures to make the neural net internally compute trigonometric functions or other representations of group elements. These works also made efforts to define progress measures for grokking based on this understanding of the final weights. In a related study, Morwani et al. 2024 derived analytical formulas for the weights of two-layer neural nets, assuming the margin is ultimately maximized. Hu et al. 2023 computed a variety of metrics throughout training and fit a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) over them to study the phase transition in grokking. A common issue with these works is that why progress measures themselves can make progress is still not well understood and requires new insights into the training dynamics, which is the focus of our work.

Dynamical Analysis of Grokking.

A few recent works were devoted to theoretically analyze the training dynamics in the grokking phenomenon. Liu et al. 2022 attributed the delayed generalization in grokking to the slow learning speed of the input embeddings. They especially analyzed the dynamics of the input embeddings in a related optimization problem, and showed that the eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix in the ODE can be used to predict the convergence. However, it is unclear how this relates to the training dynamics of the original problem and why the neural net overfits the dataset before the predicted convergence time. Žunkovič and Ilievski 2022 analyzed a simple linear classification problem, where the loss is the squared loss with explicit ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization. Assuming specific input distributions, they proved sharp transition in test accuracy and derived an estimate of the grokking time, which depends on the initialization and regularization strength. Levi et al. 2024 leveraged random matrix theory to analyze grokking in a standard linear regression setting, where the test accuracy can provably exhibit sharp transition if the accuracy is defined as the fraction of points whose regression loss is smaller than a small threshold. All these works are limited to linear models, while our work is able to analyze deep homogeneous neural nets.

Concurrent Works.

Concurrent to our work, Kumar et al. 2024 hypothesized that grokking is due to a transition from lazy to rich regimes, and observed that manipulating the scale parameter for the output and the task-model alignment between NTK and ground-truth labels can control the time to escape the lazy regime and the test accuracy when staying in the lazy regime. This observation is consistent with our work, but we provide rigorous analyses for both lazy and rich regimes with quantitative bounds. Xu et al. 2024 proved that training two-layer neural nets on XOR cluster data with noisy labels can exhibit grokking. Both their work and our work go beyond linear models, but their analysis does not show whether the transition in test accuracy is sharp or not, while our work provides quantitative bounds for the sharp transition in grokking.

Implicit Bias.

A line of works seek to characterize the implicit bias of optimization algorithms that drive them to generalizable solutions. Several forms of implicit bias have been considered, including equivalence to NTK [Du et al. 2019b, Du et al. 2019a, Allen-Zhu et al. 2019, Zou et al. 2020, Chizat et al. 2019, Arora et al. 2019b, Ji and Telgarsky 2020b, Cao and Gu 2019], margin maximization [Soudry et al. 2018, Nacson et al. 2019a, Lyu and Li 2020, Ji and Telgarsky 2020a], parameter norm minimization [Gunasekar et al. 2017, Gunasekar et al. 2018a, Arora et al. 2019a] and sharpness minimization [Blanc et al. 2020, Damian et al. 2021, HaoChen et al. 2021, Li et al. 2022, Lyu et al. 2022, Gu et al. 2023]. In this work, we characterize the early phase implicit bias based on NTK and late phase implicit bias based on margin maximization.

Appendix B Discussion: Other Implicit Biases Can Also Induce Grokking

The main paper focuses on the grokking phenomenon induced by large initialization and small weight decay, where the transition in the implicit bias is very sharp: 1−cλ​log⁡α\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha leads to the kernel predictor, but increasing it slightly to 1+cλ​log⁡α\frac{1+c}{\lambda}\log\alpha leads to a KKT solution of min-norm/max-margin problems associated with the neural net. In this section, we discuss two other possible sources of grokking: implicit margin maximization and sharpness reduction. These two sources can also cause the neural net to generalize eventually, but the transition in test accuracy is not as sharp as the case of using large initialization and small weight decay.

B.1 Implicit Margin Maximization Without Weight Decay

One may wonder if grokking still exists if we remove the small weight decay in our setting. In Liu et al. 2023, it has been argued that adding a non-zero weight decay is crucial for grokking since the weight norm has to lie in a certain range (Goldilocks zone) to generalize.

We note that for classification tasks,  Lyu and Li 2020, Ji and Telgarsky 2020a have shown that gradient descent/flow on homogeneous neural nets converges to KKT points of the margin maximization problem (R1), even without weight decay. So it is still possible that some implicit bias traps the solution in early phase, such as the implicit bias to NTK Allen-Zhu et al. 2019, zou2018stochastic, Ji and Telgarsky 2020b, Cao and Gu 2019. Then after training for sufficiently long time, the margin maximization bias arises and leads to grokking.

We empirically show that training two-layer neural nets without weight decay indeed leads to grokking, but the transition is no longer sharp. More specifically, we use the same setting as in Section 2 but with weight decay λ=0\lambda=0. We focus on analyzing the training dynamics of full-batch gradient descent with learning rate so small that the trajectory is close to the gradient flow, which ensures that gradient noise/training instability is not a potential source of implicit regularization.

However, directly training with a constant learning rate leads to very slow loss convergence in the late phase. Inspired by Lyu and Li 2020, Nacson et al. 2019b, we set the learning rate as ηℒ⁡(𝜽⁡(t))\frac{\eta}{\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}}(t))}, where η\eta is a constant. The main intuition behind this is that the Hessian of ℒ⁡(𝜽)\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}}) can be shown to be bounded by 𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(𝜽)⋅poly⁡(‖𝜽‖2))\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}})\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\|{\bm{\theta}}\|_{2})), and gradient descent stays close to gradient flow when the learning rate is much lower than the reciprocal of the smoothness. Figure 4 plots training and test curves, where xx-axis shows the corresponding continuous time calculated by summing the learning rates up to this point. It is shown that a very quick convergence in training accuracy occurs in the early phase, but the test accuracy improves extremely slowly in the late phase: the test accuracy slowly transitions from ∼0%\sim 0\% to 100%100\% as tt increases from 1010210^{10^{2}} to 1010410^{10^{4}}. In contrast, Figure 2 shows that training with weight decay leads to a sharp transition when the number of steps is ∼107\sim 10^{7}.

We note that this much longer time for grokking is not surprising, since the convergence to max-margin solutions is already as slow as 𝒪⁡(log⁡log⁡tlog⁡t)\mathcal{O}(\frac{\log\log t}{\log t}) for linear logistic regression [Soudry et al. 2018].

B.2 Sharpness Reduction with Label Noise

Grokking can also be triggered by the sharpness-reduction implicit bias of optimization algorithm, e.g., label noise SGD [Blanc et al. 2020, Damian et al. 2021, Li et al. 2022] and 1-SAM [Wen et al. 2023]. The high-level idea here is that the minimizers of the training loss connect as a Riemannian manifold due to the overparametrization in the model. Training usually contains two phases for algorithms which implicitly minimize the sharpness when the learning rate is small, where in the first phase the algorithm minimizes the training loss and finds a minimizer with poor generalization, while in the second phase the algorithm implicitly minimizes the sharpness along the manifold of the minimizers, and the model groks when the sharpness is sufficiently small. The second phase is typically longer than the first phase by magnitude and this causes grokking.

As a concrete example, Li et al. 2022 shows that grokking happens when training two-layer diagonal linear networks Equation 4 by label noise SGD (6) when the learning rate is sufficiently small. We consider the same initialization as in Section 3.2.3, where 𝜽⁡(0)=α⁡(𝟏,𝟏){\bm{\theta}}(0)=\alpha({\bm{1}},{\bm{1}}), where α>0\alpha>0 controls the initialization scale. Different from Section 3.2.3, we consider a ℓ2\ell_{2} loss, and the label is generated by a sparse linear ground-truth, that is, 𝒚∗​(𝒙)=𝒙⊤​𝒘∗{\bm{y}}^{*}({\bm{x}})={\bm{x}}^{\top}{\bm{w}}^{*}, where 𝒘∗{\bm{w}}^{*} is κ\kappa-sparse. We also assume data distribution is the isotropic Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I).

Proof.

C.3 Rich Regime

Now we proceed to prove Theorem 3.5 for the rich regime. First, we derive the following bound for the training loss at the end of the kernel regime.

Lemma C.10.

At t=1λ​(log⁡α−1L​log⁡log⁡A+Δ​T)t=\frac{1}{\lambda}(\log\alpha-\frac{1}{L}\log\log A+\Delta T), we have ℒλ​(𝛉⁡(t))=𝒪⁡(λ​(log⁡1λ)2/L)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(t))=\mathcal{O}(\lambda(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{2/L}).

Proof.

By Lemma C.4, we can easily obtain the bound

ℒ⁡(𝜽⁡(t))=𝒪⁡(log⁡AA​exp⁡(2​(L−1)​(log⁡α−1L​log⁡log⁡A)))=𝒪⁡(λ​(log⁡A)−1+2/L).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}}(t))=\mathcal{O}(\tfrac{\log A}{A}\exp(2(L-1)(\log\alpha-\tfrac{1}{L}\log\log A)))=\mathcal{O}(\lambda(\log A)^{-1+2/L}).

Also we have the norm bound ‖𝜽⁡(t)‖2=𝒪⁡(α​e−λ​t)=𝒪​(log⁡A)1/L\|{\bm{\theta}}(t)\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(\alpha e^{-\lambda t})=\mathcal{O}(\log A)^{1/L} since it is in the kernel regime. We can conclude the proof by noting that ℒλ=ℒ+‖𝜽‖22\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}=\mathcal{L}+\|{\bm{\theta}}\|_{2}^{2} and log⁡A=O⁡(log⁡1λ)\log A=O(\log\frac{1}{\lambda}).

The loss bound then implies the following norm bound.

Lemma C.11.

If ℒλ​(𝛉⁡(0))=𝒪⁡(λ​(log⁡1λ)2/L)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(0))=\mathcal{O}(\lambda(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{2/L}), then for all t≥0t\geq 0,

‖𝜽⁡(t)‖2=Θ⁡((log⁡1λ)1/L).\displaystyle\|{\bm{\theta}}(t)\|_{2}=\Theta((\log\tfrac{1}{\lambda})^{1/L}).

Proof.

For all t≥0t\geq 0, the following relationship can be deduced from the monotonicity of ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}, ri​(𝜽⁡(t))≤n​ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(t))r_{i}({\bm{\theta}}(t))\leq n\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(t)), and the Lipschitzness of fif_{i}:

Ω⁡(log⁡(1/λ))≤log⁡1n​ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(0))≤log⁡1n​ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(t))≤qi​(𝜽⁡(t))≤B0​‖𝜽⁡(t)‖2L.\displaystyle\Omega(\log(1/\lambda))\leq\log\frac{1}{n\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(0))}\leq\log\frac{1}{n\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(t))}\leq q_{i}({\bm{\theta}}(t))\leq B_{0}\|{\bm{\theta}}(t)\|_{2}^{L}.

So ‖𝜽⁡(t)‖2=Ω⁡((log⁡1λ)1/L)\|{\bm{\theta}}(t)\|_{2}=\Omega((\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{1/L}). Also note ‖𝜽⁡(t)‖22≤2λ​ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(t))≤2λ​ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(0))=𝒪⁡((log⁡1λ)1/L)\|{\bm{\theta}}(t)\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{2}{\lambda}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(t))\leq\frac{2}{\lambda}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(0))=\mathcal{O}((\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{1/L}). So we have the tight norm bound ‖𝜽⁡(t)‖2=Θ⁡((log⁡1λ)1/L)\|{\bm{\theta}}(t)\|_{2}=\Theta((\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{1/L}).

To prove Theorem 3.5, it suffices to prove the following.

Theorem C.12.

For any starting point 𝛉0​(α){\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha) satisfying ℒλ​(𝛉0​(α))=O⁡(λ​(log⁡1λ)2/L)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha))=O(\lambda(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{2/L}) and a time function T⁡(α)=Ω⁡(1λ​log⁡1λ)T(\alpha)=\Omega(\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\frac{1}{\lambda}), given any sequence {αk}\{\alpha_{k}\} with αk→+∞\alpha_{k}\to+\infty, there exists a sequence {tk}k≥1\{t_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} such that tk≤T⁡(α)t_{k}\leq T(\alpha), and every limit point of {𝛉⁡(tk,𝛉0​(αk))‖𝛉⁡(tk,𝛉0​(αk))‖2:k≥0}\{\frac{{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};{\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha_{k}))}{\|{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};{\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha_{k}))\|_{2}}:k\geq 0\} is along the direction of a KKT point of (R1).

For all α>0\alpha>0, 0≤ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(T⁡(α)))=ℒλ​(𝜽0)−∫0T⁡(α)‖∇ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(t))‖22​𝑑t0\leq\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(T(\alpha)))=\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}_{0})-\int_{0}^{T(\alpha)}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(t))\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t. Since ℒλ​(𝜽0​(α))=O⁡(λ​(log⁡A)2/L)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha))=O(\lambda(\log A)^{2/L}), we have the bound ∫0T⁡(α)‖∇ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(t))‖22​𝑑t≤𝒪⁡(λ​(log⁡1λ)2/L)\int_{0}^{T(\alpha)}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(t))\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\mathcal{O}(\lambda(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{2/L}), which implies that there exists a time τα\tau_{\alpha} such that ‖∇ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(τα))‖22≤𝒪⁡(λ2​(log⁡1λ)−(1−2/L))\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(\tau_{\alpha}))\|_{2}^{2}\leq\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{2}(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{-(1-2/L)}).

Now let tk=ταkt_{k}=\tau_{\alpha_{k}}. It suffices to prove in the case where 𝜽⁡(tk,𝜽0​(αk))‖𝜽⁡(tk,𝜽0​(αk))‖2∈𝒮d−1\frac{{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};{\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha_{k}))}{\|{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};{\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha_{k}))\|_{2}}\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1} converges; otherwise we can do the same prove for any convergent subsequence. Denote 𝜽⁡(tk,𝜽0​(αk)){\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};{\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha_{k})) as 𝜽(k){\bm{\theta}}^{(k)} and 𝜽⁡(tk,𝜽0​(αk))‖𝜽⁡(tk,𝜽0​(αk))‖2\frac{{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};{\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha_{k}))}{\|{\bm{\theta}}(t_{k};{\bm{\theta}}_{0}(\alpha_{k}))\|_{2}} as 𝜽¯(k)\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}^{(k)} for short. We claim that the limit 𝜽¯:=limk→+∞𝜽¯(k)\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}:=\lim_{k\to+\infty}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}^{(k)} is along a KKT-margin direction of (R1).

First, according to our choice of tkt_{k}, we have

‖1n∑i=1nri(𝜽(k))∇qi(𝜽(k))−λ𝜽(k)‖2≤𝒪(λ(logA)−(1/2−1/L)).\displaystyle\left\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}({\bm{\theta}}^{(k)})\nabla q_{i}({\bm{\theta}}^{(k)})-\lambda{\bm{\theta}}^{(k)}\right\|_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}(\lambda(\log A)^{-(1/2-1/L)}). (21)

By Lemma C.11, λ​‖𝜽(k)‖2=𝒪⁡(λ​(log⁡1λ)1/L)\lambda\|{\bm{\theta}}^{(k)}\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(\lambda(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{1/L}). Now we divide λ​‖𝜽(k)‖2\lambda\|{\bm{\theta}}^{(k)}\|_{2} on both sides of (21):

‖∑i=1n‖𝜽‖2L−2n​λri(𝜽(k))∇qi(𝜽¯(k))−𝜽¯(k)‖2≤𝒪((log⁡A)−(1/2−1/L)(log⁡1λ)1/L).\displaystyle\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\|{\bm{\theta}}\|_{2}^{L-2}}{n\lambda}r_{i}({\bm{\theta}}^{(k)})\nabla q_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}^{(k)})-\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}^{(k)}\right\|_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{(\log A)^{-(1/2-1/L)}}{(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{1/L}}\right). Let 𝜹⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init):=(1α​eλ​t​𝜽​(t,α​𝜽¯init)−𝜽¯init){\bm{\delta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}):=\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}e^{\lambda t}{\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})-\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right) and 𝒉⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init):=αL​e−L​λ​t​𝜹​(t,α​𝜽¯init){\bm{h}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}):=\alpha^{L}e^{-L\lambda t}{\bm{\delta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}). In the following, we show via a series of lemmas that for any 𝒗{\bm{v}} that is in the orthogonal complement of 𝚽{\bm{\Phi}}, ⟨𝜹,𝒗⟩‖𝜹‖2→0\frac{\left\langle{{\bm{\delta}}},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle}{\|{\bm{\delta}}\|_{2}}\to 0, which is a crucial property for deriving the implicit bias.

Lemma D.3.

For any vector 𝐯{\bm{v}} that lies in the orthogonal space of the column space of Φ\Phi, we have ⟨𝛅⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝛉¯init),𝐯⟩=𝒪⁡(α−2​c​L)\left\langle{{\bm{\delta}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle=\mathcal{O}\left(\alpha^{-2cL}\right) where Tc−​(α):=1−cλ​log⁡αT_{c}^{-}(\alpha):=\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha.

By update rule,

d​𝜹d​t=1αeλ​t(−2∑i=1nsi∇fi(𝜽(t;α𝜽¯init))).\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}{\bm{\delta}}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\tfrac{1}{\alpha}e^{\lambda t}\left(-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}\nabla f_{i}({\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))\right).

Then we have

=−2​1α​eλ​t​⟨∑i=1nsi​(∇fi​(𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init))−∇fi​(α​e−λ​t​𝜽¯init)),𝒗⟩\displaystyle=-2\frac{1}{\alpha}e^{\lambda t}\left\langle{\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}\left(\nabla f_{i}({\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))-\nabla f_{i}(\alpha e^{-\lambda t}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\right)},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle
=−2​αL−2​e−(L−2)​λ​t​⟨∑i=1nsi​(∇fi​(α−1​eλ​t​𝜽​(t,α​𝜽¯init))−∇fi​(𝜽¯init)),𝒗⟩\displaystyle=-2\alpha^{L-2}e^{-(L-2)\lambda t}\left\langle{\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}\left(\nabla f_{i}(\alpha^{-1}e^{\lambda t}{\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))-\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\right)},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle

where the second equation is due to our choice of 𝒗{\bm{v}} and the last equation follows from the homogeneity of fif_{i}. Now, since fif_{i} is locally smooth in a neighbourhood of 𝜽¯init\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}} and ‖1α​eλ​t​𝜽​(t)−𝜽¯init‖2=𝒪⁡(α−L)⋅eL​λ​t\left\|\frac{1}{\alpha}e^{\lambda t}{\bm{\theta}}(t)-\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\alpha^{-L}\right)\cdot e^{L\lambda t} by Lemma D.2, we have

∥∇fi(α−1eλ​t𝜽(t;α𝜽¯init)−∇fi(𝜽¯init)∥2=𝒪(α−LeL​λ​t).\|\nabla f_{i}(\alpha^{-1}e^{\lambda t}{\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})-\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\alpha^{-L}e^{L\lambda t}\right).

Let t0=120​(L−1)​λt_{0}=\frac{1}{20(L-1)\lambda}, then for t∈[0,t0]t\in[0,t_{0}], we have 1−e2​(L−1)​λ​τ≥(L−1)​λ​τ1-e^{2(L-1)\lambda\tau}\geq(L-1)\lambda\tau, so that

d​⟨𝜹,𝒗⟩d​t\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\left\langle{{\bm{\delta}}},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle}{\mathrm{d}t} =𝒪⁡(α−2​e2​λ​t​ℒ⁡(𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init)))\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\left(\alpha^{-2}e^{2\lambda t}\sqrt{\mathcal{L}\left({\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\right)}\right)
=𝒪⁡(α−2​e2​λ​t​max⁡{exp⁡(−νntk​A​λ​t16​n+λ​t),α−2​(L−1)​λ​e2​(L−1)​λ​t})\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\alpha^{-2}e^{2\lambda t}\max\left\{\exp\left(-\frac{\nu_{\mathrm{ntk}}A\lambda t}{16n}+\lambda t\right),\alpha^{-2(L-1)}\lambda e^{2(L-1)\lambda t}\right\}\right)
=𝒪⁡(max⁡{α−2​exp⁡(−νntk​A​λ​t32​n),λ​α−2​L​e2​L​λ​t})\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\max\left\{\alpha^{-2}\exp\left(-\frac{\nu_{\mathrm{ntk}}A\lambda t}{32n}\right),\lambda\alpha^{-2L}e^{2L\lambda t}\right\}\right)

for sufficiently large α\alpha, since A=α2​(L−1)λA=\frac{\alpha^{2(L-1)}}{\lambda}. On the other hand, for t∈[t0,Tc−​(α)]t\in\left[t_{0},T_{c}^{-}(\alpha)\right], the second term in (26) dominates the first term, so that

=𝒪⁡(α−2​e2​λ​t⋅α−2​(L−1)​λ​e2​(L−1)​λ​t)=𝒪⁡(λ​α−2​L​e2​L​λ​t).\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\alpha^{-2}e^{2\lambda t}\cdot\alpha^{-2(L-1)}\lambda e^{2(L-1)\lambda t}\right)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\lambda\alpha^{-2L}e^{2L\lambda t}\right).

Lemma D.4.

For 𝛉=𝛉⁡(t){\bm{\theta}}={\bm{\theta}}(t) with t≤1λ​(log⁡α+Δ​T)t\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(\log\alpha+\Delta T\right) as defined in Lemma D.2, we have

f⁡(1α​eλ​t​𝜽,𝒙)\displaystyle f(\tfrac{1}{\alpha}e^{\lambda t}{\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) =⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝜹⟩+𝒪⁡(α−L)⋅eL​λ​t​‖𝜹‖2,\displaystyle=\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{\delta}}}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-L})\cdot e^{L\lambda t}\|{\bm{\delta}}\|_{2}, (28)
f⁡(𝜽,𝒙)\displaystyle f({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{x}}) =⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝒉⟩+𝒪⁡(α−L)⋅eL​λ​t​‖𝒉‖2.\displaystyle=\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{h}}}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-L})\cdot e^{L\lambda t}\|{\bm{h}}\|_{2}. (29)

=f⁡(𝜽¯init,𝒙)+⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝜹⟩+𝒪⁡(α−L)⋅eL​λ​t​‖𝜹‖2\displaystyle=f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})+\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{\delta}}}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-L})\cdot e^{L\lambda t}\|{\bm{\delta}}\|_{2}
=⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝜹⟩+𝒪⁡(α−L)⋅eL​λ​t​‖𝜹‖2,\displaystyle=\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{\delta}}}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-L})\cdot e^{L\lambda t}\|{\bm{\delta}}\|_{2},

Lemma D.5.

‖𝒉⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init)‖2=Θ⁡(1)\|{\bm{h}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}=\Theta(1).

On the other hand, recall that Tc−​(α)=1−cλ​log⁡αT_{c}^{-}(\alpha)=\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, so by Equation 26 we have

|si|≤n​ℒ​(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))=𝒪⁡(max⁡{e−Ω⁡(A),λ​α−2​(L−1)​c})=𝒪⁡(α−2​(L−1)​c).|s_{i}|\leq\sqrt{n\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\max\left\{e^{-\Omega(A)},\lambda\alpha^{-2(L-1)c}\right\}\right)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\alpha^{-2(L-1)c}\right).

Thus, for sufficiently large α\alpha, we have |fi​(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))|≥12​yi\left|f_{i}({\bm{\theta}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))\right|\geq\frac{1}{2}y_{i}.

12​yi≤‖∇fi​(𝜽¯init)‖2​‖𝒉‖2+𝒪⁡(α−c​L)​‖𝒉‖2⇒‖𝒉‖2=Ω⁡(1)\frac{1}{2}y_{i}\leq\|\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}\|{\bm{h}}\|_{2}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-cL})\|{\bm{h}}\|_{2}\Rightarrow\|{\bm{h}}\|_{2}=\Omega(1)

as desired.

Corollary D.6.

limα→0⟨𝜹‖𝜹‖2​(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init),𝒗⟩=0\lim_{\alpha\to 0}\left\langle{\frac{{\bm{\delta}}}{\|{\bm{\delta}}\|_{2}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle=0.

Proof.

By the previous lemma, we have ‖𝜹⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init)‖2=Ω⁡(α−L​eL​λ​Tc−​(α))=Ω⁡(α−c​L)\|{\bm{\delta}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}=\Omega\left(\alpha^{-L}e^{L\lambda T_{c}^{-}(\alpha)}\right)=\Omega(\alpha^{-cL}). On the other hand, ⟨𝜹⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init),𝒗⟩=𝒪⁡(α−2​c​L)\left\langle{{\bm{\delta}}(T_{c}^{-}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle=\mathcal{O}\left(\alpha^{-2cL}\right) by Lemma D.3. The conclusion immediately follows.

Theorem D.7.

For any constant c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), letting Tc−​(α):=1−cλ​log⁡αT^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha):=\frac{1-c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, it holds that

∀𝒙∈ℝd:limα→+∞f⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init),𝒙)=⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝒉ntk∗⟩.\displaystyle\forall{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\qquad\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}f({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}});{\bm{x}})=\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}}}\right\rangle.

Proof.

By Lemmas D.5 and D.4 we have

f⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init),𝒙)\displaystyle f({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}});{\bm{x}}) (30)
=⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝒉⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))⟩+𝒪⁡(α−L)⋅eL​λ​Tc−​(α)​‖𝒉⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init)‖2\displaystyle=\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{h}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-L})\cdot e^{L\lambda T_{c}^{-}(\alpha)}\|{\bm{h}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}
=⟨∇f​(𝜽¯init,𝒙),𝒉⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))⟩+𝒪⁡(α−c​L)\displaystyle=\left\langle{\nabla f(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}};{\bm{x}})},{{\bm{h}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-cL})

By Lemma D.1 we have for ∀i∈[n]\forall i\in[n], |fi​(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))−yi|=𝒪⁡(α−2​(L−1))\left|f_{i}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))-y_{i}\right|=\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{-2(L-1)}). Since yi=⟨∇fi​(𝜽¯init),𝒉ntk∗⟩y_{i}=\left\langle{\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})},{{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}}}\right\rangle, we have

limα→+∞⟨∇fi​(𝜽¯init),𝒉⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))−𝒉ntk∗⟩=0.\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\left\langle{\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})},{{\bm{h}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))-{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}}}\right\rangle=0. (31)

By Corollaries D.6 and D.5 we have that for any direction 𝒗{\bm{v}} orthogonal to the column space of Φ\Phi, we have limα→+∞⟨𝒉⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init)),𝒗⟩=0\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\left\langle{{\bm{h}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))},{{\bm{v}}}\right\rangle=0. Combined with Equation 31, we deduce that

The above holds for all ∇fi​(𝜽¯init),i∈[d]\nabla f_{i}(\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}),i\in[d], which are exactly the columns of Φ\Phi. Note also that 𝒉ntk∗{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}} also lies in the column space of Φ\Phi, so we actually have limα→+∞‖𝑷Φ​𝒉​(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))−𝒉ntk∗‖2=0\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\|{\bm{P}}_{\Phi}{\bm{h}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))-{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}}\|_{2}=0. Hence, we can use Equation 32 to deduce that limα→+∞‖𝒉⁡(𝜽⁡(Tc−​(α),α​𝜽¯init))−𝒉ntk∗‖2=0\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\|{\bm{h}}({\bm{\theta}}(T^{-}_{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))-{\bm{h}}^{*}_{\mathrm{ntk}}\|_{2}=0. Finally, plugging this into Equation 30 gives the desired result.

D.2 Rich Regime

Now we proceed to prove Theorem 3.10 for the rich regime. First, we derive a norm bound.

Lemma D.8.

For any constant c>0c>0, let Tc+​(α):=1+cλ​log⁡αT_{c}^{+}(\alpha):=\frac{1+c}{\lambda}\log\alpha, then we have that

max1λ​log⁡α≤t≤Tc+​(α)⁡‖𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init)‖2=𝒪⁡(1).\max_{\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha\leq t\leq T_{c}^{+}(\alpha)}\|{\bm{\theta}}\left(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(1).

Proof.

We know from Lemmas D.2 and D.1 that

ℒ⁡(𝜽⁡(1λ​log⁡α,α​𝜽¯init))≤max⁡{1n​‖y‖22​exp⁡(−νntk​A16​n​(L−1)),16​n​L2​‖𝒚‖22​λ2νntk2}≤𝒪⁡(λ2).\mathcal{L}\left({\bm{\theta}}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right)\leq\max\left\{\frac{1}{n}\|y\|_{2}^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{\nu_{\mathrm{ntk}}A}{16n(L-1)}\right),\frac{16nL^{2}\|{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}\lambda^{2}}{\nu_{\mathrm{ntk}}^{2}}\right\}\leq\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{2}).

Moreover, by Lemma D.2 we know that ‖𝜽⁡(1λ​log⁡α,α​𝜽¯init)‖2=𝒪⁡(1)\|{\bm{\theta}}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(1), so that

ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(1λ​log​α,α​𝜽¯init))=ℒ⁡(𝜽⁡(1λ​log​α,α​𝜽¯init))+λ2​‖𝜽⁡(1λ​log​α,α​𝜽¯init)‖22=𝒪⁡(λ).\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}\left({\bm{\theta}}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right)=\mathcal{L}\left({\bm{\theta}}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\left\|{\bm{\theta}}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}=\mathcal{O}(\lambda).

Since {𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init)}t≥0\left\{{\bm{\theta}}\left(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right\}_{t\geq 0} is the trajectory of GF on ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}, we know that for ∀t≥1λ​log⁡α\forall t\geq\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha, we have ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init))=𝒪⁡(λ)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}\left({\bm{\theta}}\left(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right)=\mathcal{O}(\lambda) as well. This implies that ‖𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init)‖2=𝒪⁡(1)\|{\bm{\theta}}\left(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(1) as desired.

Now we prove Theorem 3.10.

Proof.

By Lemma C.5, we know that for t=1λ​log⁡αt=\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha, we have ‖𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init)−𝜽¯init‖2=𝒪⁡(1)⇒‖𝜽⁡(t,α​𝜽¯init)‖2=𝒪⁡(1)\|{\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})-\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(1)\Rightarrow\|{\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(1). Since

and 0≤ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(Tc+​(α),α​𝜽¯init)),ℒλ​(𝜽⁡(1λ​log⁡α,α​𝜽¯init))≤𝒪⁡(λ)0\leq\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}\left({\bm{\theta}}\left(T_{c}^{+}(\alpha);\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right),\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}\left({\bm{\theta}}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}\right)\right)\leq\mathcal{O}(\lambda) by Lemma D.1, we deduce that there exists tα∈[1λ​log⁡α,Tc+​(α)]t_{\alpha}\in\left[\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\alpha,T_{c}^{+}(\alpha)\right] such that ‖∇ℒλ(𝜽(t;α𝜽¯init))‖2≤𝒪(λcλlogα)=𝒪(λ(log1λ)−1/2)\left\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}({\bm{\theta}}(t;\alpha\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}}))\right\|_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\lambda}{\frac{c}{\lambda}\log\alpha}\right)=\mathcal{O}(\lambda(\log\frac{1}{\lambda})^{-1/2}).

For any sequence {αk}k≥1\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} with αk→+∞\alpha_{k}\to+\infty, we choose tk=tαkt_{k}=t_{\alpha_{k}}. By the choice of {ik}k≥1\{i_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} we know that {𝜽⁡(tik,αik​𝜽¯init)}k≥1\left\{{\bm{\theta}}(t_{i_{k}};\alpha_{i_{k}}\bar{{\bm{\theta}}}_{\mathrm{init}})\right\}_{k\geq 1} converges to a point 𝜽∗∈ℝd{\bm{\theta}}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, so the above implies that
